set1.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: A healthy 8-year-old girl has sinus arrhythmia on a sports physical. What does the finding usually mean?
opts: Sick sinus syndrome
Sick sinus syndrome is exit block, pauses and arrest together in one patient, a rare disease state; sinus arrhythmia is benign.
Sinus node disease
Variation that follows breathing reflects vagal tone, not a diseased node; sinus arrhythmia is benign.
A benign normal variant
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia, also called respiratory sinus arrhythmia, is a benign condition and is most commonly seen in children.
An atrioventricular block
Atrioventricular blocks change the PR or drop QRS complexes; sinus arrhythmia keeps normal PR and every QRS.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 81

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 33-year-old man's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is his ventricular rate?
opts: 110 per minute
One hundred ten would be eleven complexes in six seconds; there are thirteen here, giving 130.
130 per minute
Correct. Thirteen QRS complexes fall in the six seconds, and thirteen times ten is 130 per minute.
150 per minute
One hundred fifty would need fifteen complexes; thirteen times ten is 130 per minute.
65 per minute
Sixty-five halves the count; the six-second method multiplies thirteen complexes by ten, giving 130.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 47
set1.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with tick marks at the start, middle and end, and regularly spaced narrow complexes.

set1.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
set1.q: A 68-year-old man feels tired; his strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm runs 60 to 100 per minute; R waves here are about six large boxes apart, just over 50.
Sinus bradycardia
Correct. The rhythm is regular and slow, about 51 per minute, with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes and a normal PR interval.
Sinus pause
A sinus pause breaks an otherwise steady rhythm with one gap; here every R to R interval is the same, just long.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops a cycle and leaves a gap; this strip is regular, merely slow.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 75, 77
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with three widely spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, at equal intervals.

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 66-year-old man's ST segment is being compared with baseline. Which segment best shows the true isoelectric line?
opts: The PR segment
The impulse is crossing the atrioventricular node during the PR segment; the TP segment is the true resting baseline.
The ST segment
The ST segment is what is being compared, the ventricles holding their contraction; the reference is the TP segment.
The QT interval
The QT interval is all ventricular activity, not a baseline; the TP segment is the resting reference.
The TP segment
Correct. The TP segment, from the end of the T wave to the next P wave, is the resting state and the best place to assess the isoelectric line.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 68-year-old man is placed on a cardiac monitor. Why is lead II used for rhythm interpretation?
opts: It views the heart's vector
Correct. Lead II has a perfect view of the heart's vector, which is why it is the lead used for rhythm interpretation.
It sits over the sinoatrial node
No electrode sits over the sinoatrial node; lead II is chosen because it looks straight along the heart's vector.
It is the only bipolar lead
Leads I, II and III are all bipolar; lead II is chosen for its view along the heart's vector.
It shows the septum best
The septal wall is viewed by V1 and V2; lead II is chosen for its view of the overall vector.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 25, 27

set1.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: An 81-year-old woman's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus pause
A sinus pause is a shorter reset gap; once at least three cycles are missed, as here, it is sinus arrest.
Sinus exit block
In exit block the gap is an exact multiple of the cycle and beats march out; this gap does not.
Sinus arrest
Correct. The node stops and starts again, and the flat gap spans well over three missed cardiac cycles; the beats after it do not march out.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia never leaves a long flat gap; it varies the spacing gradually.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 95, 99, 100
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with four narrow complexes, a long flat baseline several cycles wide, then four more complexes.

set1.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: A 66-year-old man has sinus exit block. How do his P waves look when present?
opts: Inverted before each QRS
Inverted P waves point to a junctional origin; the beats in sinus exit block are normal sinus beats.
Normal and married to the QRS
Correct. In sinus exit block, sinus pause and sinus arrest the P waves, when present, are normal and married to the QRS complexes; whole cycles are simply missing.
Of three different shapes
Three P wave shapes describe a wandering atrial pacemaker; exit block beats share one normal sinus P wave.
Replaced by flutter waves
Flutter waves replace P waves in atrial flutter; exit block keeps normal P waves on the beats present.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 86, 92

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 79-year-old woman has lost both sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodal function. Which structure now paces her heart?
opts: Bundle of His
The bundle of His conducts the impulse from the atrioventricular node to the bundle branches; the third pacemaker is the Purkinje network.
Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle is the main route of conduction between the atria; it is not the backup to the two nodes.
Purkinje network
Correct. The Purkinje network is the heart's third pacemaker, taking over when both nodes fail, at 20 to 40 per minute.
Middle internodal tract
The internodal tracts connect the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes; the pacemaker after both nodes is the Purkinje network.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 14, 15

set1.io: Recognize normal sinus rhythm
set1.q: A 50-year-old woman's strip is shown. Which feature points to the sinoatrial node as the pacemaker?
opts: Identical upright P waves
Correct. A P wave married to every QRS means an atrial origin, and upright P waves of one shape point to the sinoatrial node; differing shapes point to other atrial sites.
Narrow QRS complexes
A narrow QRS shows normal ventricular conduction, which junctional rhythms can share; uniform upright P waves show the sinus origin.
A rate under 100
Rate alone does not locate the pacemaker; uniform upright P waves before each QRS identify the sinoatrial node.
A flat TP segment
The TP segment shows the resting baseline, not the pacemaker; uniform upright P waves show a sinus origin.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 57, 72
set1.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip with evenly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small rounded upright wave.

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 30-year-old woman's impulse reaches her Purkinje fibers. What is distinctive about how they conduct?
opts: They conduct fastest of all
Correct. The Purkinje network conducts action potentials more quickly and efficiently than any other cells of the conduction system.
They conduct slowest of all
Slowing belongs to the atrioventricular node, which holds the impulse; the Purkinje network is the fastest conductor.
They conduct only backward
The Purkinje network carries the impulse forward into the ventricles, faster than any other conducting cell.
They conduct only atrially
The Purkinje network lies in the ventricles, at the end of the bundle branches, and conducts fastest of all.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 14

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 39-year-old man's tracing shows a tall deflection. On electrocardiogram paper, what does the vertical axis measure?
opts: Time
Time runs along the horizontal axis, left to right; the vertical axis is voltage.
Voltage
Correct. Up and down on the paper measures voltage; moving left to right measures time.
Heart rate
Heart rate is worked out from intervals along the time axis; the vertical axis is voltage.
Paper speed
Paper speed is fixed at 25 millimeters per second along the horizontal axis; height is voltage.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 26

set1.io: Review ECG lead placement
set1.q: A 63-year-old man's finding appears in two leads that look at the same area. What are such leads called?
opts: Augmented leads
Augmented leads are aVR, aVL and aVF (augmented vector right, left and foot), made from one physical lead; leads viewing one area are contiguous.
Contiguous leads
Correct. Contiguous leads are two or more leads that look at the same area of the heart, such as II, III and aVF (augmented vector foot).
Bipolar leads
Bipolar leads are I, II and III, named for their two poles; leads that view one area are contiguous.
Precordial leads
Precordial leads are the six chest leads; leads looking at the same area are called contiguous.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 70

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 70-year-old man's lead V1 tracing is shown; each QRS is wider than three small boxes. What does this width indicate?
opts: Abnormal ventricular conduction
Correct. A normal QRS is narrow, under 0.12 seconds (three small boxes); a wider complex means conduction through the ventricles is abnormal.
Normal ventricular conduction
Normal ventricular conduction gives a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds; this complex is wider than that.
A prolonged PR interval
The PR interval is measured before the QRS, from P onset; QRS width reflects ventricular conduction.
A normal Q wave
A Q wave is only the first negative deflection and must be under 0.04 seconds; the whole complex here is too wide.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 31, 61
set1.alt: Lead V1 tracing of three beats, each with a broad notched upright complex followed by an inverted wave.

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman's strip is shown, and its R to R intervals vary. Which rate method suits it best?
opts: The 1500 method
The 1500 method divides by the small boxes of a single R to R interval, so it misleads when intervals vary.
The six-second method
Correct. The six-second method counts every complex across six seconds, so it still works when R to R intervals vary; the box-counting methods use a single interval.
The 300 method
The 300 method divides by the large boxes of one R to R interval, so it misleads in an irregular rhythm.
The count-down method
Counting down heavy lines from one R wave to the next reads only one interval and is unreliable when they vary.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 48, 52
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with narrow complexes whose spacing varies noticeably from one beat to the next.

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 47-year-old woman has a normal heart. Where is the only place an impulse can pass from her atria to her ventricles?
opts: The atrioventricular septum
The atrioventricular septum is the nonconductive wall that blocks passage; impulses cross only through the bundle of His.
Bachmann's bundle
Bachmann's bundle connects the right and left atria; it does not reach the ventricles.
The bundle of His
Correct. A nonconductive atrioventricular septum separates atria from ventricles, so in a normal heart the bundle of His is the only path.
The coronary sinus
The coronary sinus is a landmark near the atrioventricular node, not a conduction path into the ventricles.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 11, 15

set1.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: A 64-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus exit block
In exit block the gap is a whole multiple of the P to P interval; this gap is about one and a half cycles, because the node reset.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is evenly slow throughout; here a steady rhythm is broken by one long gap.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia changes the spacing gradually with breathing; this is one sudden flat gap.
Sinus pause
Correct. The node stops firing and starts again, and the next beat does not fall on the marched-out schedule, because the cycle has reset: a sinus pause.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 91
set1.alt: Line drawing of a rhythm strip without grid: five narrow complexes with small upright waves before them; one longer flat stretch separates the second and third beats.

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 47-year-old woman's regular strip is shown; consecutive R waves sit four large boxes apart. What is the rate by the 300 method (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: 60 per minute
Sixty would be five large boxes apart; at four large boxes the rate is 300 divided by four, 75.
100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; four large boxes gives 75 per minute.
75 per minute
Correct. The 300 method divides 300 by the large boxes between consecutive R waves: 300 divided by four is 75 per minute.
150 per minute
One hundred fifty would be two large boxes apart; four large boxes gives 75.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 53
set1.alt: Lead II rhythm strip on green grid paper with evenly spaced narrow complexes and small tick marks along the bottom.

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
set1.q: A 7-year-old boy's heart rate rises each time he inhales. What causes the rise?
opts: A rise in vagal tone
More vagal tone would slow the heart, as happens on exhalation; inspiration suppresses vagal tone.
Blocked sinus impulses
Blocked impulses drop whole cycles (sinus exit block); sinus arrhythmia is rate variation from vagal tone.
Suppression of vagal tone
Correct. Inspiration lowers intrathoracic and arterial pressure, the baroreceptors respond, vagal tone is suppressed and the heart rate increases.
Higher intrathoracic pressure
Intrathoracic pressure falls on inspiration, not rises; that drop leads to suppressed vagal tone.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 81

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 61-year-old man has many cells capable of automaticity. What normally keeps the lower ones from firing?
opts: The atrioventricular septum
The atrioventricular septum blocks conduction between atria and ventricles; the pacemaker hierarchy suppresses spontaneous firing.
Constant vagal stimulation
Vagal tone changes the rate (as in sinus arrhythmia) but does not explain the suppression; the pacemaker hierarchy does.
Closed calcium channels
Calcium channels open in the plateau of every action potential; the lower pacemakers are held off by the pacemaker hierarchy.
The natural pacemaker hierarchy
Correct. Spontaneous activity of other cells is prevented by the natural hierarchy of pacemaker function, with the sinoatrial node in charge.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 16

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 61-year-old woman's strip is shown; her PR intervals fall outside the normal 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. Which can cause this?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia varies the R to R interval with breathing but keeps a normal PR; blocks, accessory pathways and alternate pacemakers change the PR.
Sinus tachycardia at rest
Sinus tachycardia raises the rate with a normal PR interval; an atrioventricular nodal block can move it outside the range.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm by definition has a constant PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; nodal blocks change it.
Atrioventricular nodal block
Correct. Atrioventricular nodal blocks, accessory pathways and alternate pacemaker sites within the heart can put the PR interval outside its normal range.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 59
set1.alt: Lead II strip with brackets under the PR intervals of successive beats and one P wave labeled on its own.

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
set1.q: A 75-year-old woman's strip shows sinus exit block. What is her sinoatrial node doing during the missing cycle?
opts: Firing, but blocked
Correct. In sinus exit block the sinus node fires as normal, but the impulse is blocked from leaving it, so a cardiac cycle is absent.
Not firing at all
A node that stops firing and restarts is a sinus pause or arrest; in exit block it fires but the impulse is blocked.
Resetting its own timing
Resetting is what makes a sinus pause; in exit block the node keeps its timing, so beats march out.
Firing faster than normal
Faster firing would raise the rate; in exit block the node fires normally but the impulse does not exit.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 85
set1.alt: Monitor strip with narrow complexes and the gaps labeled underneath in seconds: 1.1, 1.0, 2.2 and 1.0.

set1.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
set1.q: A 24-year-old woman's monitor shows this strip. What is the rhythm?
opts: Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is 60 to 100 per minute; R waves two large boxes apart give 150.
Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia is irregular and 60 to 100 per minute; this strip is regular and fast.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is below 60 per minute; this strip runs at about 150.
Sinus tachycardia
Correct. The rhythm is regular at about 150 per minute (R waves two large boxes apart), with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 78, 80
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with closely and evenly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small wave before it.

set1.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: A 10-year-old girl with sinus arrhythmia breathes in deeply. What happens to her heart rate?
opts: It decreases
The rate falls on exhalation, not inspiration; breathing in speeds it up.
It pauses briefly
No beat is dropped in sinus arrhythmia; the rate simply rises on inspiration.
It increases
Correct. On inspiration the heart rate rises, and on exhalation it falls; the rate follows the breathing.
It stays fixed
A fixed rate would be normal sinus rhythm; in sinus arrhythmia it rises on inspiration.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 81

set1.io: Apply a systematic approach to ECG interpretation
set1.q: A 45-year-old man's strip has been assessed for rate, regularity, P waves and PR interval. What is the final step?
opts: The rate
Rate is the first step, not the last; the systematic approach ends with the QRS.
The QRS
Correct. The five steps are rate, regularity, P waves, PR interval and QRS; the QRS (narrow under 0.12 seconds, or wide) comes last.
The T wave
The T wave is not one of the five systematic steps; the approach ends with the QRS.
The axis
Axis belongs to 12-lead interpretation; the five rhythm steps end with the QRS.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 42

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman's strip is assessed with R to R and P to P intervals. What are these intervals used for?
opts: Rate, regularity, heart blocks
Correct. R to R and P to P intervals are used to assess rhythm rate and regularity and also to assess heart blocks.
QRS width and ST changes
QRS width is measured across the complex and ST changes against the TP baseline; the intervals give rate, regularity and blocks.
Lead placement and wiring
Placement is checked against the anatomical landmarks; the intervals assess rate, regularity and heart blocks.
Axis and chamber enlargement
Axis comes from the limb leads; R to R and P to P intervals assess rate, regularity and heart blocks.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 41

set1.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set1.q: A 36-year-old man is studied for a reentry rhythm. In most people, which internodal tract truly attaches to the atrioventricular node?
opts: The middle tract
The middle tract usually terminates somewhere within the right atrium; it is the fast, superior anterior tract that attaches.
The inferior posterior tract
The inferior posterior (slow) tract usually ends within the right atrium; in most people only the fast tract attaches.
All three, equally
There are three internodal pathways, but in most people only the superior anterior (fast) tract reaches the atrioventricular node.
The superior anterior tract
Correct. In most people only the superior anterior tract, the fast tract, truly attaches to the atrioventricular node; the other two end in the right atrium.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set1.q: A 52-year-old man's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is his ventricular rate?
opts: 80 per minute
Eighty would be eight complexes in six seconds; this strip carries nine, so the rate is 90.
100 per minute
One hundred would need ten complexes in six seconds; there are nine here, giving 90.
60 per minute
Sixty would be six complexes; nine QRS complexes in six seconds times ten is 90 per minute.
90 per minute
Correct. Nine QRS complexes fall between the three-second markers, and nine times ten is 90 per minute (the six-second method).
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 45
set1.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with three-second tick marks along the top and regularly spaced narrow complexes.

set1.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set1.q: A 74-year-old man is evaluated for sick sinus syndrome. Which sinus node problems does the condition group together?
opts: Three degrees of heart block
First-, second- and third-degree blocks are delays or failures in the atrioventricular node or below; sick sinus syndrome is a disorder of the sinus node itself.
Exit block, pause and arrest

Correct. Sick sinus syndrome is the umbrella for sinus node problems such as sinus exit block, sinus pause and sinus arrest, often more than one in the same patient, even on one strip. It is mostly a disease of older adults.
Premature beats from three sites
Premature atrial, junctional and ventricular beats are ectopic beats arising outside the sinus node; sick sinus syndrome is a group of sinus node problems.
Fascicular and bundle branch blocks
Fascicular and bundle branch blocks are ventricular conduction delays below the atrioventricular node; sick sinus syndrome is a disorder of the sinus node itself.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 101

set1.io: Review ECG lead placement
set1.q: A 58-year-old woman's augmented leads are recorded. What do augmented leads use as their negative pole?
opts: A central terminal in the heart
Correct. Augmented leads use one physical lead and a theoretical negative pole that the machine places in the center of the heart, the central terminal, so they are unipolar.
The right leg electrode
The right leg electrode is a ground; augmented leads use the central terminal as their negative pole.
The left shoulder electrode
The left shoulder carries the positive pole of aVL (augmented vector left); the negative pole is the central terminal.
A chest electrode
Chest electrodes are themselves unipolar leads; the augmented leads' negative pole is the central terminal.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 64

set1.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
set1.q: A healthy 9-year-old boy has this strip at a routine visit. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia
Correct. Every complex has a normal P wave married to a narrow QRS with a normal PR, but the R to R intervals vary: sinus arrhythmia, a benign finding most common in children.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm is regular; here the R to R intervals lengthen and shorten.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops a whole cycle, leaving one gap that marches out; here intervals vary gradually.
Sinus pause
A sinus pause is a single sudden gap; here the spacing shifts gradually across the strip.
set1.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 81, 82, 84
set1.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks and narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, with gaps that vary in length.

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 72-year-old man's regular strip is shown; his R waves sit about six large boxes apart. What is his rate closest to (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: About 50 per minute
Correct. By the 300 method, 300 divided by six large boxes is 50 per minute (this strip measures about 51), below 60 and so a bradycardia.
About 75 per minute
Seventy-five would be four large boxes apart; six large boxes gives about 50 per minute.
About 100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; six large boxes gives about 50.
About 30 per minute
Thirty would be ten large boxes apart; at six large boxes the rate is about 50 per minute.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 77
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with three widely spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, at equal intervals.

set2.io: Apply a systematic approach to ECG interpretation
set2.q: A 41-year-old man's P waves are described as married to the QRS complexes. What does married mean?
opts: All P waves look alike
Uniform shape is a separate question (same morphology); married means each P wave is causing its QRS.
Each P wave causes its QRS
Correct. Married P waves are the ones causing the QRS complexes: one P before each QRS, at a constant PR interval.
P waves sit on T waves
A P wave on a T wave would be early and abnormal; married means each P wave causes the QRS after it.
Two P waves per QRS
Two P waves per QRS means some do not conduct; married means one P wave causing each QRS.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 57, 58

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 41-year-old man's strip is printed at the standard 25 millimeters per second. How long is one small box?
opts: 0.2 seconds
That is one large box, made of five small boxes; a single small box is 0.04 seconds.
0.04 seconds
Correct. Each small box is 1 millimeter tall and 0.04 seconds (40 milliseconds) wide, not 0.04 milliseconds.
0.004 seconds
That is ten times too short; at 25 millimeters per second each 1 millimeter box is 0.04 seconds.
0.4 seconds
That is two large boxes; one small box at standard speed is 0.04 seconds.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 33-year-old woman's ventricular cell is at rest in phase 4. What is the voltage inside the cell?
opts: About −70 millivolts
The phase 4 resting value is lower, about −90 millivolts, the level the cell returns to at the end of phase 3.
About 0 millivolts
Zero is passed during the upstroke, not at rest; the resting cell sits at about −90 millivolts.
About +30 millivolts
A positive inside is the depolarized state after sodium rushes in; at rest the inside is about −90 millivolts.
About −90 millivolts
Correct. At rest, with more potassium inside and sodium and calcium outside, the inside of the cell sits at about −90 millivolts.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 18, 22

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 52-year-old woman's sinoatrial impulse must reach her left atrium. Which structure is the main route?
opts: Bundle of His
The bundle of His connects the atrioventricular node to the bundle branches; atrium-to-atrium conduction runs through Bachmann's bundle.
Left bundle branch
The left bundle branch enters the left ventricle, not the left atrium; Bachmann's bundle links the two atria.
Inferior posterior tract
The inferior posterior tract is an internodal pathway toward the atrioventricular node; Bachmann's bundle reaches the left atrium.
Bachmann's bundle
Correct. Bachmann's bundle extends from the right to the left atrium and is the main route of interatrial conduction.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 57-year-old woman's myocytes are contracting. During which action potential phase does calcium enter the cell?
opts: Phase 2, the plateau
Correct. In phase 2 calcium channels open and calcium entering the cell causes contraction; the voltage holds level, giving the plateau.
Phase 0, the upstroke
Phase 0 is fast sodium influx; calcium enters later, in the phase 2 plateau.
Phase 1, the notch
Phase 1 is early repolarization as sodium channels close; calcium channels open in phase 2.
Phase 4, the rest
Phase 4 is diastole, with calcium outside the cell; it enters in phase 2.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 20, 21

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman's monitor prints this six-second strip. What is her ventricular rate?
opts: 140 per minute
Correct. Fourteen QRS complexes in six seconds, multiplied by ten, gives a ventricular rate of 140 per minute.
120 per minute
One hundred twenty would be twelve complexes; the strip carries fourteen in six seconds, so 140.
70 per minute
Seventy halves the count; fourteen complexes in six seconds times ten is 140 per minute.
160 per minute
One hundred sixty would need sixteen complexes; fourteen in six seconds gives 140.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 44, 46
set2.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with three-second tick marks above and many closely spaced narrow complexes.

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 48-year-old woman's lead V1 tracing is shown, and its complexes look broad. What duration defines a normal QRS?
opts: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds
That is the normal PR interval; a QRS of 0.12 seconds or more is abnormal ventricular conduction.
Less than 0.12 seconds
Correct. The QRS duration must be less than 0.12 seconds, under three small boxes.
Less than 0.04 seconds
That is the limit for a normal Q wave alone; the whole QRS must be under 0.12 seconds.
0.35 to 0.45 seconds
That is roughly the QT interval in males (350 to 450 milliseconds); the QRS must be under 0.12 seconds.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 31, 60, 61
set2.alt: Lead V1 tracing of three beats, each with a broad notched upright complex followed by an inverted wave.

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 28-year-old man reviews one cardiac action potential beginning at rest. In what order do the phases run?
opts: The numbers do not run in order from rest: rest is phase 4, which comes before the phase 0 upstroke.
Phase 1 follows the upstroke rather than starting the cycle; from rest the order is 4, 0, 1, 2, 3.
Repolarization (3) comes last, not second; from rest the order is 4, 0, 1, 2, 3.
Correct. The cycle starts at rest in phase 4, then the upstroke (0), the notch (1), the plateau (2) and rapid repolarization (3).
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22

set2.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
set2.q: A 31-year-old man's regular strip is shown; R waves sit two large boxes apart. What is the rate (normal 60 to 100 per minute)?
opts: 100 per minute
One hundred would be three large boxes apart; two large boxes gives 150.
300 per minute
Three hundred would be an R wave on every large box; two boxes apart halves that to 150.
75 per minute
Seventy-five would be four large boxes apart; two large boxes gives 150 per minute.
150 per minute
Correct. By the 300 method, 300 divided by two large boxes is 150 per minute; with sinus P waves that is sinus tachycardia.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 52, 80
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with closely and evenly spaced narrow complexes, each with a small wave before it.

set2.io: Recognize sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia
set2.q: A 12-year-old girl's strip is shown. Which feature separates her rhythm from normal sinus rhythm?
opts: Absent P waves
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a normal P wave before every QRS; only the regularity differs.
A rate over 100 per minute
Over 100 per minute is sinus tachycardia; sinus arrhythmia runs 60 to 100 but irregularly.
Irregular R to R intervals
Correct. Sinus arrhythmia meets all the sinus criteria (60 to 100 per minute, normal married P waves, normal PR) but its R to R intervals are irregular.
A prolonged PR interval
The PR stays normal, 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; what differs is the irregular R to R.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 82, 84
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with three-second tick marks and narrow complexes, each preceded by a small upright wave, with gaps that vary in length.

set2.io: Interpret electrocardiographic findings for sinus rhythms: sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set2.q: A 78-year-old man's strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus pause
In a sinus pause the node resets, so the gap is not a whole multiple of the cycle; this gap is two cycles and the beats march out.
Sinus arrest
Sinus arrest misses at least three cycles and resets; here a single cycle drops and the rhythm resumes on time.
Sinus exit block
Correct. The long gap measures two normal cycles, so the next beat lands on schedule and the P to P intervals march out: the node fired, but one impulse was blocked.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is evenly slow with no missing cycle; here the spacing is steady except for one dropped cycle.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 85, 89, 90
set2.alt: Pink grid strip of narrow complexes with small upright waves before each; one longer flat stretch separates the third and fourth beats.

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 45-year-old man's PR interval is measured. What span does the PR interval cover?
opts: End of P to start of QRS
That shorter span, without the P wave, is the PR segment; the interval includes the P wave.
Start of QRS to end of T
That is the QT interval, all ventricular activity; the PR interval ends where the QRS begins.
End of T to the next P
That is the TP segment, the resting state; the PR interval runs from P onset to QRS start.
Onset of P to start of QRS
Correct. The PR interval runs from the onset of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS, as the impulse crosses the atrioventricular node, His bundle and bundle branches.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 30, 27

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman's strip is shown. How is its regularity best described?
opts: Regular
A regular rhythm has the same R to R interval every beat; here consecutive gaps clearly differ.
Regular with one pause
One isolated gap in an otherwise even strip would suggest a dropped cycle; here the R to R intervals vary throughout.
Regular but slow
Slow describes the rate, not regularity; the R to R intervals here are unequal, so it is irregular.
Irregular
Correct. The R to R intervals differ from beat to beat (the gaps between consecutive complexes are visibly unequal), so the rhythm is irregular.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 54, 56
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with narrow complexes whose spacing varies noticeably from one beat to the next.

set2.io: Review ECG lead placement
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman's leads I, II and III form Einthoven's triangle. Why are they called bipolar leads?
opts: They use a central terminal
A theoretical central terminal as the negative pole is what makes the augmented and chest leads unipolar.
Each needs two physical poles
Correct. Leads I, II and III need physical positive and negative poles on the patient, so they are the bipolar leads.
They view the heart horizontally
The horizontal view comes from the precordial leads; the limb leads are bipolar because of their two physical poles.
The machine creates them
The machine creates the augmented leads from one physical lead; the bipolar leads each use two physical electrodes.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 62

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 58-year-old woman's six-second strip is shown. How is her atrial rate found from it?
opts: Count QRS complexes, multiply by ten
That gives the ventricular rate; the atrial rate uses the P waves counted in six seconds.
Divide 300 by the P waves
The 300 method divides 300 by large boxes between waves, not by a count; the atrial rate is P waves times ten.
Count P waves, multiply by ten
Correct. In the six-second method, P waves counted in six seconds times ten give the atrial rate; QRS complexes times ten give the ventricular rate.
Count T waves, multiply by ten
T waves are ventricular repolarization; the atrial rate comes from the P waves in six seconds.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 44
set2.alt: Six-second rhythm strip with three-second tick marks along the top and regularly spaced narrow complexes.

set2.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set2.q: A 57-year-old woman asks how normal sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia and sinus tachycardia differ. What separates them?
opts: The P wave shape
All three share normal, uniform P waves from the sinoatrial node; only the rate separates them.
The PR interval
All three keep a normal PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds; the rate is what differs.
The regularity
All three are regular; irregularity with sinus P waves is sinus arrhythmia.
The rate alone
Correct. All three are regular with normal P waves married to the QRS and a normal PR; only the ventricular rate (under 60, 60 to 100, over 100) differs.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 72, 75, 78

set2.io: Review ECG lead placement
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman's septal wall is in question. Which leads look at the septum?
opts: V3 and V4
V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall of the left ventricle; the septum is V1 and V2.
V5 and V6
V5 and V6 join I and aVL (augmented vector left) on the lateral wall; the septum is V1 and V2.
V1 and V2
Correct. V1 and V2 look at the septal wall; V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall beside it.
II and III
Leads II and III join aVF (augmented vector foot) on the inferior wall; the septum is V1 and V2.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 69

set2.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set2.q: A 79-year-old woman's strip is shown; her sinus node stops and restarts. What separates sinus arrest from sinus pause?
opts: P to P intervals march out
Neither pause nor arrest marches out, because the node resets; marching out is sinus exit block.
At least three missed cycles
Correct. Both reset the node and neither marches out; sinus arrest is the one in which at least three cardiac cycles have been missed.
A blocked sinus impulse
A blocked impulse is sinus exit block; pause and arrest are the node stopping, separated by the number of missed cycles.
A wide QRS after the gap
The returning beats are sinus beats with narrow QRS; the difference is three or more missed cycles.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 95
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with four narrow complexes, a long flat baseline several cycles wide, then four more complexes.

set2.io: Recognize normal sinus rhythm
set2.q: A 34-year-old woman's routine strip is shown. What is the rhythm?
opts: Sinus arrhythmia
Sinus arrhythmia has the same P waves but irregular R to R intervals; this strip is regular.
Normal sinus rhythm
Correct. The rhythm is regular, at about 75 to 80 per minute, with normal P waves married to narrow QRS complexes and a normal, constant PR.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is below 60 per minute; this strip's rate is about 75 to 80.
Sinus exit block
Sinus exit block drops whole cycles, leaving gaps; this strip has no missing beats.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 72, 73
set2.alt: Single-lead rhythm strip with evenly spaced narrow complexes, each preceded by a small rounded upright wave.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of sinus node dysfunction
set2.q: A 67-year-old woman's strip shows a sinus pause. Why do the P to P intervals fail to march out after the gap?
opts: The sinoatrial node resets
Correct. During a sinus pause the node stops firing and starts back up, so the cardiac cycle is reset and the P to P intervals no longer march out.
The impulse is blocked
A blocked impulse is sinus exit block, where the node keeps time and beats do march out.
An atrial focus takes over
The beats after the pause still have the same sinus P waves; the sinus node has simply reset.
The atrioventricular node fails
Atrioventricular failure would leave P waves without QRS complexes; in a pause the sinus node itself stops and resets.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 91
set2.alt: Line drawing of a rhythm strip without grid: five narrow complexes with small upright waves before them; one longer flat stretch separates the second and third beats.

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 71-year-old man is paced only by his Purkinje network. What intrinsic rate should be expected?
opts: 40 to 60 per minute
That is the atrioventricular node's rate; the Purkinje network, one level lower, runs at 20 to 40 per minute.
60 to 100 per minute
That is the sinoatrial node's rate; each pacemaker lower in the system is slower, and the Purkinje network runs at 20 to 40.
20 to 40 per minute
Correct. The Purkinje network, the secondary backup pacemaker, has an intrinsic rate of 20 to 40 beats per minute.
100 to 120 per minute
A lower pacemaker never runs faster than the one above it; the Purkinje network's own rate is 20 to 40 per minute.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 14, 15

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 34-year-old man's strip is shown. How is its regularity best described?
opts: Irregular
An irregular rhythm has unequal R to R intervals; on this strip they are equal throughout.
Regular
Correct. The same distance separates every pair of consecutive R waves, so the rhythm is regular.
Regular with one pause
No beat is missing; every R to R interval on this strip is the same.
Irregular when breathing
That describes sinus arrhythmia's varying R to R intervals; here every interval is equal.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 54, 55
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with tick marks at the start, middle and end, and narrow complexes spaced at equal distances.

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman's myocardium responds when a stimulus reaches it. Which property is this?
opts: Automaticity
Automaticity is producing an impulse of one's own; responding to an arriving stimulus is excitability.
Excitability
Correct. Excitability is the cardiac cell's ability to respond to an impulse or stimulus.
Conductivity
Conductivity is passing the impulse on from myocyte to myocyte; responding to it is excitability.
Contractility
Contractility is the cell's ability to contract; the electrical response to a stimulus is excitability.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Compare and contrast sinus rhythms: sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, sinus arrhythmia, sinus block, sick sinus syndrome
set2.q: A 76-year-old man has a regular rate of 52 per minute (normal 60 to 100) with wide QRS complexes. What still makes the rhythm sinus?
opts: Married normal P waves
Correct. What makes a rhythm sinus is normal P waves present and married to the QRS complexes; sinus bradycardia and tachycardia may have narrow or wide QRS.
The slow ventricular rate
Rate separates bradycardia from tachycardia but does not prove a sinus origin; married normal P waves do.
The regular R to R
Junctional and ventricular rhythms are regular too; the sinus origin shows in normal P waves married to each QRS.
The wide QRS complexes
A wide QRS reflects abnormal ventricular conduction, not the pacemaker; married normal P waves make it sinus.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 75, 78

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 46-year-old man's ventricular cell depolarizes in phase 0. Which ion movement produces this upstroke?
opts: Calcium rushing in
Calcium enters in phase 2, the plateau, where it causes contraction; the upstroke is the fast sodium influx.
Potassium leaving
Potassium outflow repolarizes the cell in phases 1 to 3; the phase 0 upstroke is sodium influx.
Sodium rushing in
Correct. In phase 0 fast sodium channels open and a rapid influx of sodium makes the inside of the cell positive.
Chloride rushing in
Chloride is not part of the cardiac action potential as taught here; phase 0 is the rapid influx of sodium.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 53-year-old woman's strip is read at standard speed. How long is one large box?
opts: 0.2 seconds
Correct. A large box is five small boxes, 5 millimeters tall and 0.2 seconds wide.
0.04 seconds
That is a single small box; five of them make one large box of 0.2 seconds.
0.5 seconds
That is two and a half large boxes; each large box is 0.2 seconds.
1 second
One second takes five large boxes; each large box is 0.2 seconds.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Review cardiac conduction system anatomy and physiology
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman's ventricular cell is in phase 3, rapid repolarization. Which ion movement returns it to its resting voltage?
opts: Potassium leaving the cell
Correct. Calcium channels close and potassium flows out of the cell, which makes the inside negative again; potassium efflux is what repolarizes the cell.
Potassium entering the cell
Moving positive potassium inward would make the inside more positive, not less; repolarization is potassium flowing out of the cell.
Calcium entering the cell
Calcium channels close in phase 3; calcium entry is the phase 2 plateau that causes contraction.
Sodium entering the cell
Sodium influx is the phase 0 upstroke; in phase 3 the cell repolarizes as potassium leaves it.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 17, 22

set2.io: Review determination of: heart rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, QTc interval
set2.q: A 74-year-old man's lead II strip is shown, with the PR intervals bracketed. What is the PR interval doing?
opts: Lengthening until a beat drops
Correct. Each PR interval is longer than the one before until a P wave stands alone without a QRS; the PR interval is not constant across the strip.
Constant across the strip
A constant PR would measure the same at every bracket; here each is longer than the last until a QRS drops.
Shortening before each beat
The brackets get wider, not narrower, until a P wave is left with no QRS.
Varying at random
The change is progressive, each PR longer than the last, ending in a dropped QRS, not random variation.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slide 59
set2.alt: Lead II strip with brackets under the PR intervals of successive beats and one P wave labeled on its own.

set2.io: Review ECG lead placement
set2.q: A 56-year-old man's inferior wall is in question. Which leads look at the inferior wall?
opts: V1 and V2
V1 and V2 look at the septal wall; the inferior leads are II, III and aVF.
V3 and V4
V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall of the left ventricle; the inferior leads are II, III and aVF.
II, III and augmented vector foot
Correct. Leads II, III and aVF (augmented vector foot) look at the inferior wall.
I, augmented vector left, V5, V6
Leads I, aVL (augmented vector left), V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall; the inferior wall is II, III and aVF.
set2.cite: 11. Rhythm Analysis and Sinus Rhythm.pptx, Slides 69, 70
